stem: Which of the following should you check FIRST when you receive a new dataset before doing any modelling?

options.text: Train a baseline model immediately to establish performance
Shape, data types, missing values, and target distribution
Run PCA to reduce dimensionality
Normalise all numeric features to [0, 1]

explanation_after: EDA always starts with basic inspection: shape (how many rows/columns), dtypes (numeric vs categorical), missing values per column, and the target distribution. Silent data issues — class imbalance, unexpected nulls, wrong types — will break any downstream model if not caught first.

stem: You plot a boxplot of 'fare' in the Titanic dataset and see several points far above the upper whisker. What is the most responsible next step?

options.text: Immediately drop all values above the upper whisker
Replace them with the median
Investigate whether they are legitimate extreme values before deciding what to do
Log-transform the column and never look at the outliers again

explanation_after: Outliers may be data entry errors, sensor failures, or legitimate extreme values (a very wealthy passenger really did pay much more). Drop before investigating loses real signal. The correct process is: identify → investigate → then decide (cap, transform, keep, or drop).

stem: You notice that the 'cabin' column in the Titanic dataset is missing for 77% of passengers, and those missing values correlate with lower passenger class. This missingness is best described as:

options.text: MCAR — Missing Completely at Random
MAR — Missing at Random (dependent on observed variables like pclass)
MNAR — Missing Not at Random (dependent on the missing value itself)
A data entry error that should be ignored

explanation_after: MAR means missingness is related to observed data (pclass), not to the missing value itself. Lower-class passengers rarely had cabin assignments, so the probability of 'cabin' being missing depends on the observed 'pclass'. This means simple mean imputation will be biased — you should create an 'cabin_missing' indicator feature.

stem: PCA is applied to a dataset with 50 features. The first two principal components explain 73% of the variance. What do the 'loadings' of PC1 tell you?

options.text: Which samples are outliers in the PCA space
How much variance each original feature contributes to PC1 — showing which features drive that dimension
The correlation between PC1 and the target variable
The explained variance ratio of PC1

explanation_after: Loadings (from pca.components_[0]) show how each original feature maps onto PC1. A large absolute loading means that feature strongly influences PC1's direction. This lets you interpret PC1 as, for example, 'size dimension' or 'malignancy dimension' in a medical dataset.

stem: How does UMAP differ from PCA for dimensionality reduction?

options.text: UMAP is always faster and produces better results than PCA in every case
PCA is linear and maximises global variance; UMAP is non-linear and preserves both local and global neighbourhood structure
PCA requires labelled data; UMAP works without labels
UMAP uses kernel methods; PCA cannot handle non-linear data

explanation_after: PCA finds orthogonal linear directions of maximum variance — it's interpretable and deterministic but misses non-linear structure. UMAP learns a low-dimensional graph that preserves local neighbourhoods (nearby points stay near) and global topology. UMAP is better for visualisation of complex manifolds; PCA is better when you need interpretable linear combinations.

stem: SHAP values are used in a Data-Centric AI workflow. What do SHAP values reveal that a simple correlation-with-target analysis cannot?

options.text: The statistical significance of each feature
Per-prediction explanations: how much each feature pushed a specific prediction higher or lower, plus interaction effects
Whether features are normally distributed
The multicollinearity between features

explanation_after: Correlation gives a global average relationship. SHAP gives a per-instance, directional decomposition: for THIS specific passenger, 'female' pushed survival probability up by 0.3, 'pclass=3' pushed it down by 0.2. Dependence plots then reveal non-linear interactions — how one feature's effect changes with another feature's value.

stem: During EDA, you discover your binary classification target is imbalanced: 98% class 0, 2% class 1. Which downstream modelling decision does this discovery directly justify?

options.text: Ignoring accuracy as the primary metric in favour of precision, recall, or F1, and considering techniques like class weighting or resampling
Doubling the size of the dataset to fix the imbalance automatically
Switching to unsupervised learning since the labels are unreliable
Removing the minority class entirely to simplify the problem

explanation_after: With 98/2 imbalance, a model predicting 'class 0' for everything scores 98% accuracy while being useless. EDA surfacing this imbalance is what should trigger choosing metrics sensitive to the minority class (precision/recall/F1/AUC) and considering class weights, oversampling (e.g. SMOTE), or undersampling during training — decisions made before modelling because EDA revealed them.

stem: During EDA you compute the mean and standard deviation of a feature using the ENTIRE dataset (train + test combined), then use those statistics to standardise all the data before splitting into train/test. What is wrong with this workflow?

options.text: Nothing — mean and std are properties of the data, not the model, so this is safe
It causes data leakage: information from the test set, via the combined mean/std, influences preprocessing applied to the training set, making evaluation results overly optimistic
It makes training slower
Standardisation should never be used before splitting, only after

explanation_after: Any statistic computed for preprocessing (mean, std, min/max, PCA components, imputation values) must be fit only on the training set, then applied — transform, not fit — to the test set. Fitting on combined data lets test-set information subtly leak into the numbers used to prepare training data, inflating test performance in a way that won't hold up on truly new, unseen data. This is one of the most common and dangerous mistakes in real ML pipelines.
